title: Burst sculpting latency-cost clipboard
body:
Purpose:
This is a working sketch of the 'burst sculpting' experiment set — lightweight collateral to help eng, product and SRE compare latency vs cost tradeoffs when intentionally shaping short-term request arrival patterns. Not a final report: quick numbers, ASCII charts, and actionable knobs for the console UI and Optimize recommendations.

Summary (one-paragraph):
Burst sculpting holds incoming requests for a short, bounded window to increase batching and prefix reuse. The net effect: modest increases to p50 latency but large savings on per-token cost during microbursts. In these experiments (small generative workloads with median request length ~60 tokens) a 30ms hold produced ~18% cost reduction at p90 latency +12ms, while a conservative 100ms hold produced ~32% cost reduction but shifted p99 by ~40–80ms depending on model. Tradeoffs vary significantly by model architecture and quantization profile.

Experimental matrix (short):
- Workloads: conversational prompt stream (~60 tokens median), small completions (~30 tokens), and multi-turn chat (avg 4 turns).
- Models: redwood-7b-q4 (opt quantized), redwood-13b-q5, open-7b-fp16 (baseline).
- Regions/hardware: core region (A100-like), edge region (A10x-like).
- Sculpt policies tested:
  * opportunistic: no hold (baseline)
  * hold-30ms: micro-hold 30ms, batch up to 32 requests or 15KB
  * hold-100ms: aggressive hold 100ms, batch up to 128 requests or 60KB
  * adaptive: start 10ms, double until latency budget exhausted (caps at 80ms)

Key quantitative table (ASCII):
Note: latencies in ms, cost = $ per 10k tokens (approx infra + amortized model cost). Measurements collected over 30-minute steady-state runs with injected bursts; p50/p90/p99 are request-to-first-token (RFT).

+----------------+------------+---------+---------+---------+----------------+
| Model          | Policy     | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | $/10k tokens   |
+----------------+------------+---------+---------+---------+----------------+
| redwood-7b-q4  | opportunistic| 45     | 92      | 210     | 12.8           |
| redwood-7b-q4  | hold-30ms   | 57     | 104     | 246     | 10.5           |
| redwood-7b-q4  | hold-100ms  | 86     | 126     | 320     | 8.7            |
+----------------+------------+---------+---------+---------+----------------+
| redwood-13b-q5 | opportunistic| 78     | 158     | 380     | 18.4           |
| redwood-13b-q5 | hold-30ms   | 95     | 172     | 420     | 15.1           |
| redwood-13b-q5 | hold-100ms  | 131    | 215     | 540     | 12.6           |
+----------------+------------+---------+---------+---------+----------------+
| open-7b-fp16   | opportunistic| 52     | 108     | 260     | 16.2           |
| open-7b-fp16   | hold-30ms   | 66     | 125     | 296     | 13.9           |
| open-7b-fp16   | hold-100ms  | 91     | 174     | 378     | 11.4           |
+----------------+------------+---------+---------+---------+----------------+

Observations (bulleted):
- Cost slope: moving from opportunistic -> hold-30ms cuts per-token cost by ~15–20% across models; hold-100ms yields another ~15–20% on top but with larger tail latency exposure.
- Latency impact: p50 shifts noticeably (10–60ms) but remains acceptable for most non-interactive flows. p99 inflation is nonlinear and model-dependent (heavier models see larger p99 shifts).
- Model sensitivity: quantized redwood-7b-q4 benefits the most in terms of cost leverage (smaller per-token baseline cost), while open-7b-fp16 has higher baseline token cost and correspondingly higher absolute savings but smaller relative gains.
- Region/hardware: on edge hardware the batching headroom is lower; hold windows should be reduced (recommend halving hold times compared to core).
- Adaptive policy: tends to capture ~90% of the cost benefits of the fixed 100ms hold while keeping p99 closer to the 30ms policy; best for mixed-latency SLAs.

Small ASCII chart: percent cost reduction vs hold duration (redwood-7b-q4)
(hold ms on x axis)
0ms |######################### 0%
30ms|######################## 18%
60ms|############################ 25%
100ms|################################ 32%

SLA impact table (quick):
- Interactive chat (SLA target p90 < 120ms): hold-30ms acceptable for redwood-7b-q4 and open-7b-fp16 in core regions; redwood-13b-q5 fails at p90 if hold-100ms is used.
- Background batch (async): hold-100ms recommended to maximize cost savings; consider per-customer opt-in.

Operational considerations and failure modes:
- Backpressure: holding introduces queuing; ensure we have queue depth caps and circuit breakers to prevent request pile-up under large sustained bursts.
- Multi-tenant fairness: sculpting increases transient concurrency; combine with slot reservations or rate-limits per-tenant to avoid noisy neighbor amplification.
- Observability: add a "sculpting" dimension to tracing (hold-time, batch-size, policy) and surface p99 deltas by tenant.
- Rollout suggestion: dark-launch adaptive policy on 5% of traffic for 72 hours; monitor p90/p99 + user-facing error rates.

UI/Optimize product recommendations (what Optimize could suggest automatically):
- If measured burstiness > X (e.g., 95th arrival-rate delta > 3x baseline), recommend hold-30ms with a predicted cost delta and expected p90/p99 shift.
- Expose fast slider: conservative (10–30ms), balanced (30–60ms), aggressive (60–120ms) with model-aware guidance.
- Per-tenant opt-in: provide per-route override and a simulated "preview" that shows projected cost/latency changes based on recent traces.

Action items / next experiments:
1) Run a longer 24-hour mixed-workload run to validate p99 tails under realistic diurnal patterns (owner: Evan).
2) Edge hardware sweep: halved hold windows + lower batch caps (owner: Priya).
3) Implement adaptive policy prototype in runtime and A/B vs fixed-30ms (owner: Tom).
4) UX copy & sandbox recommendation mockups for Optimize console (owner: Aisha).

Notes and open questions (quick):
- Need to quantify user-visible quality regressions (truncated generations due to early tokenization variance) — we saw rare artifacts when batches contain widely different sequence shapes.
- Pricing model: how should per-tenant saved $ be reported when using shared Dedicated capacity (report gross infra delta and let billing map to committed units)?

Appendix: short methodology notes
- All runs use synthetic arrival traces sampled from recent production histograms (anonymized) to recreate common microburst shapes (single-origin spike, multi-origin overlapped spike).
- Measurements collected at client-observed RFT; infra-side metrics (GPU busy, batch sizes, KV hit rates) correlated in the runs and archived in the linked PR.
- Cost model: includes amortized GPU time + energy estimate + per-GiB network egress estimate; numbers are illustrative not billing-grade.

If you want a cleaned slide deck or a short one-pager for sales, I can convert this into 3 slides: (1) what is burst sculpting + visual, (2) key numbers and recommended policies, (3) rollout/playbook.

-- Aisha
